o: Split the digits of num into two numbers (digits reusable in any order, leading zeros allowed) minimizing their sum. For 4325 the best is 24 + 35 = 59; for 687 it is 68 + 7 = 75. Intuitively we want both numbers to have nearly equal digit counts and the smallest digits in the most significant positions.
k: To minimize a sum of two numbers built from fixed digits, balance their lengths and put small digits first.
Sorting digits ascending and dealing them alternately achieves both goals greedily.

a.i: Sort the digits ascending. Assign them alternately to num1 and num2 (smallest digit to num1, next to num2, and so on). This keeps the two numbers' lengths within one of each other and places the smallest digits at the highest-value positions of each number, which is an exchange-argument-optimal assignment.
s: Extract and sort the digits of num ascending.
Append digits alternately to num1 and num2.
Return the integer sum of the two resulting numbers.
a.t: O(d log d) where d is the number of digits (≤ 10) — sorting dominates.

w: An exchange argument proves optimality: if a larger digit sits at a more significant position than a smaller one in the same number, swapping them never increases the sum; balancing lengths minimizes the total positional weight. Edge cases include repeated digits and numbers whose optimal split puts a leading zero in one part (handled naturally). A follow-up might ask for three-way splits, where the same greedy extends.
